structure.overview: The case concerns Adeyinka Ilori's judicial review of a Citizenship Judge's decision denying his Canadian citizenship application due to insufficient residence evidence and credibility concerns. The Federal Court found the tribunal record incomplete and illegible, and that a natural justice breach occurred because Mr. Ilori was not given a fair opportunity to respond to adverse evidence. The court granted judicial review, set aside the decision, and ordered a rehearing by a new decision maker.

party_points.text: natural justice breach and error in evidence assessment
Applicant was informed of evidence and had opportunity to respond
self-represented applicants must know the case to meet and respond fairly
Citizenship Judge applied a qualitative test not clearly communicated
failure to inform Applicant of test applied and case to meet breaches natural justice
declines to certify question on document retention, governed by Privacy Regulations

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Applicant, Adeyinka Ilori, entered Canada in 2010, became a permanent resident, and applied for citizenship in 2013, defining the relevant residence period.

summaries.speaker: below
summaries.summary: The Citizenship Judge denied Mr. Ilori's citizenship application due to insufficient evidence of residence and credibility concerns.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Ilori did not receive the Citizenship Judge's decision until 2.5 years later, after which he filed for judicial review; Justice Barnes accepted this timeline.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: Mr. Ilori's judicial review raises issues of natural justice breach and error in evidence assessment, plus a preliminary issue about the tribunal record's completeness.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court finds the tribunal record incomplete and illegible, and a natural justice breach occurred, so it grants judicial review and orders rehearing.
idea_list: Grant of judicial review and rehearing

summaries.speaker: other
summaries.summary: Annex A contains the applicable legislative provisions relevant to the case.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Procedural fairness breaches are reviewed on a correctness standard focusing on fairness and justice, citing Canadian Pacific Railway and Vavilov.
idea_list: Standard of review for procedural fairness

citations.cite: Canadian Pacific Railway Company v Canada (Attorney General), 2018 FCA 69 at para 54
citations.why: States correctness standard for procedural fairness breaches

citations.cite: Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at para 77
citations.why: Explains procedural fairness is context-specific and flexible

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The presumptive standard of review is reasonableness, requiring justification and rationality, with the challenger bearing the onus, per Vavilov.

citations.why: States presumptive standard of review is reasonableness
Defines reasonableness as coherent and rational analysis
Challenger must show decision is unreasonable

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The tribunal record is incomplete and missing key documents central to the Citizenship Judge's decision, preventing meaningful judicial review.

citations.cite: Togtokh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 581 at para 16
citations.why: Supports setting aside decision due to incomplete record

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Two versions of the tribunal record were submitted; the second includes a typed transcript and is clearer and more complete, and is accepted by the court.

citations.cite: Federal Courts Citizenship, Immigration and Refugee Protection Rules, SOR/93-22 [IMM Rules], Rule 17

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The typed transcript improves legibility but remains incomplete with undecipherable parts, raising questions about the original hearing notes' clarity.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Several key documents referenced by the Citizenship Judge are missing from both versions of the tribunal record.

citations.why: Defines residence requirement relevant to documents

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Additional documents attached to Mr. Ilori's affidavit are missing from the tribunal record, including hearing notices and responses to information requests.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The missing documents prevent meaningful judicial review; passport stamps are not conclusive but were inconsistently accepted by the Citizenship Judge.

citations.cite: Haddad v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 976 at para 24
citations.why: Passport stamps not irrefutable proof of entries/exits

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Missing documents and illegible hearing notes impede review; notes should be legible to assist in assessing decision rationality per Vavilov.

citations.why: Reasonableness requires rational chain of analysis

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Respondent admitted documents were destroyed after microfilming; this risks setting aside decisions if central documents are lost prematurely.

citations.why: Regulates retention and destruction of personal information

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Despite the record issues being determinative, the court addresses the natural justice breach to avoid repetition on rehearing.

summaries.speaker: party
summaries.summary: The Respondent argues Mr. Ilori was informed of evidence and had opportunity to respond, but the court disagrees.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Citizenship Judge's decision discusses evidence without showing it was put to Mr. Ilori at hearing; the court finds no indication he was questioned on it.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court agrees with the Applicant that evidence was used to discredit him without giving a fair chance to respond, breaching natural justice.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: Information from Mr. Ilori’s spouse suggesting he lives in Nigeria was not put to him at hearing, though it may have influenced the Judge’s decision.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Applicant accepts the Minister's investigative powers, but the court stresses self-represented applicants must know the case to meet and respond fairly.

citations.cite: Fazail v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2016 FC 111 at para 46
citations.why: Duty of procedural fairness requires knowing the case to meet

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Citizenship Judge shifted from a quantitative to a qualitative test, focusing on Mr. Ilori’s living and working in Nigeria, which was not clearly communicated.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court explains three citizenship tests exist, including the qualitative Koo test, and procedural fairness requires applicants know which test applies; the Judge applied a veiled Koo test.

citations.cite: Miji v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 142 at para 19

citations.why: Defines qualitative test focusing on residence location
Procedural fairness requires applicant know test applied

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The Citizenship Judge failed to inform Mr. Ilori of the test applied and the case to meet, breaching natural justice.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court grants judicial review, sets aside the Citizenship Judge’s decision, and orders rehearing by a new decision maker.

summaries.speaker: court
summaries.summary: The court declines to certify the Applicant’s proposed question on document retention, finding it not dispositive and governed by Privacy Regulations.

citations.why: Governs document retention of personal information
